lesson.title: Mass Spectrometry: Weighing Individual Atoms and Molecules
lesson.summary: Mass spectrometry is an analytical technique that ionizes, accelerates, and deflects charged particles to measure their mass-to-charge ratio and relative abundance with high precision.
lesson.body:
Average atomic mass calculations depend on knowing two things about every isotope of an element: its exact atomic mass and its natural abundance. Mass spectrometry is the instrument technique that measures both of these directly and with remarkable precision, and it is how essentially every average atomic mass value on the periodic table was determined in the first place. A mass spectrometer works in four basic stages: vaporization, ionization, acceleration and deflection, and detection, each one engineered to separate particles by their mass-to-charge ratio, written m over z.

In the first stage, a sample is vaporized into a gas of individual atoms or molecules if it is not gaseous already. In the second stage, ionization, a beam of high-energy electrons is fired at these gas-phase particles, knocking one or more electrons off each one and leaving behind positively charged ions, most commonly with a single positive charge. This step matters because only charged particles can be steered and measured using electric and magnetic fields, the tools the rest of the instrument depends on; a neutral atom would pass straight through undeflected and undetectable.

In the third stage, these positive ions are accelerated through a strong electric field, giving every ion roughly the same kinetic energy regardless of its mass. The ion beam then passes through a magnetic field oriented to bend the beam's path. Because all the ions carry the same kinetic energy but different masses, the magnetic field deflects lighter ions more sharply than heavier ones, exactly the way a lighter ball curves more than a heavier one thrown with the same force. This deflection separates the original mixed sample into distinct beams, one for each different mass-to-charge ratio present in the sample.

In the final stage, a detector positioned at the end of the flight path records how many ions of each mass-to-charge ratio arrive, converting that count into an electrical signal. The result is a mass spectrum, a plot of ion abundance against mass-to-charge ratio, with a separate peak for each isotope or fragment present in the sample. For an element with several stable isotopes, this produces one peak per isotope, with the height, or more precisely the area, of each peak proportional to how much of that isotope was actually present in the sample, which is exactly the relative abundance data needed for average atomic mass calculations.

A concrete worked example: when neon gas is analyzed by mass spectrometry, the spectrum shows a tall peak at mass-to-charge ratio 20, a very small peak at 21, and a moderate peak at 22, corresponding to the isotopes neon-20, neon-21, and neon-22. From measured peak areas, chemists determine the abundances are approximately 90.5 percent, 0.3 percent, and 9.2 percent respectively. Multiplying each isotope's mass by its abundance and summing, following the average atomic mass method, reproduces neon's periodic table value of about 20.18 u. This is not a coincidence: mass spectrometry is precisely how that periodic table value was originally measured, and reading a spectrum like this to extract abundances and calculate an average mass is exactly the skill built next in mass spectrum analysis.
